text:
Droit de la famille — 131448

2013 QCCS 3177

JD 2422

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

LAVAL

No:

540-12-014150-080

DATE:

May 14, 2013

______________________________________________________________________

IN THE PRESENCE OF:

THE HONOURABLE

SYLVIE DEVITO, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

K. R.

Plaintiff

v.

M. V.

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

REASONS OF THE JUDGMENT RENDERED
FROM THE BENCH

ON MAY 10, 2013

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The Court was seized of three motions:

A.

mother’s amended motion in modification of accessory measures pursuant
to a judgment of the Court of appeal and for provision for costs, dated  March
25, 2013;

B.

father’s amended motion to have mother’s pleadings declared improper
and to impose sanctions, dated March 28, 2013;

C.

father’s motion to modify accessory measures with respect to spousal
support, dated March 29, 2011.

[
2
]

Seeing that the three days allotted for the
hearing, beginning on April 17, would not have sufficed to complete the
presentation of the evidence and arguments on all matters, the parties agreed
that priority should be given to the issue of custody.

[
3
]

Although defendant began to initiate proof as
pertains to the issue of improper use of proceedings, after careful
consideration, and given the time constraints, the Court decided that it would
be more appropriate that the issues of improper use of proceedings, provision
for costs and spousal support be debated together subsequently.

[
4
]

Therefore, the hearing on these issues was
deferred to the next best available date, February 20 and 21, 2014.

[
5
]

Consequently, the Court is now seized with the
sole issue of custody.

THE PROCEEDINGS

[
6
]

The parties were married in 1998 and separated
in 2008.

[
7
]

Two children were born from this union: X, who
is now 13 and Y, now 11.

[
8
]

Divorce proceedings were introduced by the
mother in 2008. This has unfortunately been a very acrimonious divorce and a
bitter battle from the outset.

[
9
]

Between April 2008 and the divorce judgment of
June 23, 2009, at least nine judgments were rendered: several interim orders, a
judgment on provisional measures and a judgment finding the mother in contempt
of Court. Appeals from the two latter were also filed.

[
10
]

Initially, the mother was granted custody and
the father visitation rights. However, the situation deteriorated and the
father was prevented from exercising his rights by the mother. Contempt of Court
charges were laid, she was found guilty and appealed. The condemnation was
maintained.

[
11
]

On June 23, 2009, Borenstein J. who pronounced
the divorce, awarded the custody of the children to the father after finding
that the mother had an alienating behaviour towards the father.

[
12
]

She concluded that it was urgent that all
contacts between the mother and the children be stopped. This judgment was
appealed by the mother. It was later confirmed in January 2010 by the Court of
appeal, except as concerns the modalities determined by Borenstein J.
pertaining to the issue of resumption of access rights by the mother.

[
13
]

At that point, the children had already started
therapy in 2009 with Dr Abe Worenklein.

[
14
]

Only a few days after the Court of appeal judgment,
the mother filed a motion to modify accessory measures which is basically the
motion now before this Court.

[
15
]

After Borenstein J.’s findings and before the
judgment of the Court of appeal was rendered, eventually, at the suggestion of
the children’s therapist, visitation with the mother resumed by way of supervised
access, on a once a week basis, for a period of two hours. This continued for
about two years, from 2009 unto 2011.

[
16
]

In September 2011, at the urging of our
colleague Fournier J., as he then was, the parties agreed to a joint psychosocial
expertise.

[
17
]

Notwithstanding the mother’s initial opposition,
again voiced in proceedings, the parties finally agreed to implement the
expert’s recommendation that the visitation rights of the mother gradually increase
and become unsupervised. Monitoring of the situation was to be continued and an
additional report was to be filed by the same expert in time for the new
hearing date scheduled in April 2012.

[
18
]

Unfortunately, because of inexplicable
circumstances, at that date, the expert had not received a formal request to prepare
his complementary report. The request was then filed and the trial postponed
yet another time to April 2013.

[
19
]

In the meantime, access rights increased
slightly, by consent of the parties.

[
20
]

However, in the fall of 2012, the mother sought
assistance from another attorney and again seized the court with further
interim requests to modify custody or access rights, notwithstanding the fact
that the case was already scheduled for a hearing in April 2013 and that the
parties were awaiting the additional expert report.

[
21
]

She claimed this was at the children’s urging.
The children were asked to sign affidavits outlining grievances concerning
their father. He countered the request and the mother was ultimately unsuccessful
in these new attempts.

[
22
]

The court is now seized with the mother’s recently
amended motion to modify accessory measures which, as mentioned above,
initially dates back from January 2010.

[
23
]

Three years have lapsed since the mother filed
her initial motion to modify accessory measures. Turn of events, combined with
numerous motions, several court orders and court delays bring this Court to
again, revisit the situation.

[
24
]

When the initial accessory measures were
pronounced, the children were respectively 9 and 7. As mentioned above, they
are now 13 and 11.

[
25
]

At this time the children enjoy unsupervised visits
with their mother on Saturdays, from 1 pm unto Sunday 5 pm, 3 weekends out of
4.

[
26
]

The mother now requests that she be granted either
full custody, shared custody or enlarged visiting rights.

[
27
]

The mother’s motion raises the following question:
are there new elements which justify the Court to modify the accessory measures
as pertains to custody of the parties’ children? And if so, what is in the best
interest of the children.

THE EVIDENCE

[
28
]

This Court heard both parents, the father’s new
girlfriend, Mr Alain Blais, the expert who prepared the psychosocial reports
filed in the record, both children (who incidently had also been heard by Borenstein
J. in 2009). The Court also read Dr Abe Worenklein's reports filed in the
record.

[
29
]

On this last issue, at the outset and by mutual
consent, both parents and their attorneys had agreed to be provided with
progress reports from Dr Worenklein. It appears that X knew of this, but that Y
may not have been made aware.

[
30
]

It should be mentioned that the children are now
counselled and represented by an attorney, Me Molpeceres, who was only appointed
on March 19, 2013 following yet another motion from the mother. He warned about
the fact that the therapy reports were circulated among the parties and
questioned whether this would jeopardize the therapeutic relationship between
Dr Worenklein and the children.

[
31
]

Seeing that such was the mutual intent at the
outset of establishing psychological support for the children and that the
reports where indeed filed in the record, the Court concluded it was relevant
to take cognizance of such.

[
32
]

Therefore, having carefully considered the
evidence as a whole, the following observations can be made by the Court.

-

The mother

[
33
]

At this time she does not work. The father still
supports her. As indicated, the issue of maintaining or not spousal support
will be debated before the Court at a later date.

[
34
]

The Court believes the mother when she states "that
her children are her life". She loves them and has the capacity to care
for them.

[
35
]

However, her absence of recognition of the
father’s role in the children’s lives is still very present. It is particularly
obvious when asked twice, by two different attorneys, to mention three
qualities that the father may have, or to describe his role as a father: she
remains speechless and does not answer. To this purpose, she is at the exact
same stage as when questioned by Borenstein J. in 2009.

[
36
]

She is not very convincing when she states that
the children should see their father: in fact, when asked hypothetically what
type of visitation she would offer if she were granted custody, she fails to
provide any suggestion.

[
37
]

It is evident that since 2009, the mother has
not evolved significantly in understanding the importance of the role of the
father in the children’s lives. She does not seem to recognize that the children
have done very well on many levels since the father was awarded custody.

[
38
]

The Court is convinced that she does love the children
and wishes to spend more time with them. What is somewhat less apparent, is whether
her motion concerns her own needs rather than those of the children.

[
39
]

She has received some psychological support
which she states helped her to cope with the absence of her children. However,
she still has not gained insight on the issue of alienation, nor about the
consequences to the children that such a behaviour entails.

-

The father

[
40
]

He also loves his children. He has been the main
parental figure for the last four years.

[
41
]

Although very controlled in his testimony when
relating the events during this period as pertains to the mothers’ behaviour,
the Court cannot help but sense that he is exasperated. He may very well sometimes
have trouble keeping this sentiment to himself, keeping his frustration to
himself and not sharing it with the children. This should be avoided.

[
42
]

However, the evidence shows that he has tried to
be flexible and that he is very sensitive to his daughters’ needs and wishes as
concerns their mother’s role.

[
43
]

He is very credible when he explains the
important place the mother must have in their lives and how open he is to share
the responsibilities with her if she were able to recognize his input.  He is
also very convincing when he explains his distress at the possibility of
loosing the children if custodial arrangements are not carefully put in place
to avoid further alienation.

[
44
]

The fact that the children are thriving in most
areas of their lives demonstrates that his parental capacities are undeniable.

-

The children

[
45
]

Both are intelligent, surprisingly well adapted
and resilient, considering the difficult situation they have endured for the
last five years.

[
46
]

They are doing extremely well in school and
socially, although they state that they miss their friends having recently
moved from Town A where they used to live. Their good performance in school has
however not been altered by the move. For X, it has been a significant
improvement since she has been victim to bullying in her prior school.

[
47
]

Both children express love for their parents. However,
they both insist they miss their mother and wish to spend more time with her.
Their attorney voices their wish to live with her.

[
48
]

X, the eldest, is very vocal and outgoing. When
asked about the family situation, in an exasperated way, she volunteers that
she is “caught in the middle”.

[
49
]

What struck the Court is that although she says
she still wants to see her father, it seems that to be with her mother means that
her relationship with her father becomes of less importance. For her, the fact
that she has “time to catch up“ with her mother equates a necessity to choose,
as if sharing time is not conceivable.

[
50
]

However, she appears at ease to speak her mind
to both parents.

[
51
]

On the other hand, Y, who is younger, expresses
the wish to have a balanced relationship with both parents. She is less
expansive than X, and expresses a lot of sadness when it comes to missing her
mother. She appears more subdued.

[
52
]

When asked, both children spontaneously and
sincerely voice qualities they attribute to both parents. However, they both
state they are more comfortable with their mother, for certain things.

-

The experts

[
53
]

Mr Blais has filed two reports: one in January
2011 by which he recommended progressively resuming unsupervised visitation rights
for the mother, with a complementary report to be conducted in six months.
After an initial refusal by the mother, these recommendations were finally
agreed to and implemented.

[
54
]

Mr Blais’ follow-up report is dated April 11,
2013. After meeting the parents, both children, and contacting Dr Worenklein,
he formulates the following opinion:

[…]

The
effects of the situation initially observed appear to have diminished, as the
children are more capable of expressing their opinion regarding their family
situation. It is observed that Y and X maintain a high level of complic-

ity with their mother, while also
recognizing their father’s commitment towards them. Nevertheless, it is still
preoccupying that the both children maintain that they were victim of physical
abuse from their father, which was considered unfounded by the professionals
who assessed the situation at the time. As well, the children appear to
describe their situation with the same words and explanations as their mother.

Both Y and X expressed their wish
to live with their mother, feeling that she would be in a better position to
ensure their development and best interest. I believe that a change of custody
could potentially estrange them from their father, as there are still elements
of badmouthing present (threatening to move in a smaller apartment if they do
not live with her, not allowing them to participate in father’s family events,
open contacts between her and the children through email and Facebook, etc.)
and considering that Ms R. is unable to explain how she would maintain contacts
between the children and their father. In this context, the contacts between
the children and their mother should be limited to recommended accesses,
excluding email and Facebook contact.

Finally, it is still comforting to
witness that the children have been able to thrive in this context, and that
they have been able to maintain a steadfast relationship with both parents,
although still appear to be aligned with their mother’s position.

[
55
]

Mr Blais recommends the following access
arrangement:

-

that custody remain with the father;

-

that access rights be exercised by the mother
three weekends out of five, from Saturday 9 am to Sunday 5 pm, including a
holiday occurring before or after that period;

-

that the mother be allowed to contact the
children by phone once a week, on Wednesday, between 7 and 7:30 pm or otherwise
agreed by the parents;

-

that e-mail, facebook and texting communications
be excluded because they encourage continued intervention by the mother during
custodial time of the father;

-

that the children spend two consecutive weeks
with their mom during the summer;

-

that they be allowed to travel with their father
for two consecutive weeks to Mexico during the Holiday season;

-

and he goes on to suggest modalities for sharing
other holidays.

[
56
]

When pressed by Me Molpeceres on the issue of whether
increasing the weekend period with the mother by one or two nights is
appropriate, although reluctantly, Mr. Blais concedes this could be envisioned.
He explains that the idea of suggesting three weekends out of five would allow
the father to dispose of more than one weekend to explore further leisure activities
with his dauthers, which the actual arrangement prevents him from doing.

[
57
]

As for Dr Worenklein, according to the reports
filed in the record, he met with the children six times between June 29 and
August 14, 2009, then more sporadically between September and December 2009
while supervised access arrangements were resuming. He again reported in
February and May 2010. Interventions on his part, if any, are not documented in
the record for 2011. Basically, this is when unsupervised access rights resumed
progressively after Mr Blais’ initial report.

[
58
]

Dr Worenklein’s reports dated October 29 and
November 26, 2012 were also filed. They were given at a time of crisis, when
the mother initiated motions to modify the custody and when affidavits were
signed by the children.

[
59
]

His most recent report is dated April 16, 2013.

[
60
]

Over this four-year period, Dr Worenklein has
met with the children and also with the parents, lately more sporadically. His
reports do state that the children have consistently requested to spend more
time with their mother.

[
61
]

He confirms the existence of parental alienation
on the part of the mother. He has been counselling the children in dealing with
this issue while providing insight to the parents on the consequences of such
behaviour, by means of forwarding his reports to them.

[
62
]

He expressed concern when made aware of the
affidavits signed by the children in the fall of 2012. He stated that "
therapy,
in terms of helping the children adjust to their parents’ situation will
continue to be negatively impacted upon as long as they are enmeshed in the
conflict and exposed to negative information about one or both of their parents.
"

He concludes that "
they clearly are conflicted as a result of their
having been triangulated between their parents and overburdened as a result.
"

[
63
]

In his most recent report, Dr Worenklein is
still weary of Mr Blais’ findings concerning the children’s complicity with
their mother and the fact that they would still restate events pertaining to
alledged abuse by the father, using the same words as the mother. He confirms
his commitment to protect his professional relationship with his patients and
to respect their wish to not disclose certain information. However, he assures
that should he have been told information indicating that the children were at
a serious risk, he would have reported such to the Youth Protection Department.

DECISION

[
64
]

As mentioned above, the Court must first decide
if since the last judgment, there have been changes which warrant a
modification to the existing custodial arrangement.

[
65
]

The main change is that since the introduction
of the mother’s motion in 2010, three years have lapsed. Three years during which
many events occurred.

[
66
]

But mainly, seeing that the children have gone
from 9 to 13 for X and from 7 to 11 for Y, or put otherwise, have become adolescent
and pre-adolescent, this in itself constitutes a significant change.

[
67
]

This was not the case when the mother's motion
was initially introduced in 2010.

[
68
]

The Court finds, as do the experts, that the
children have gained some insight and seem to be able to distance themselves
from their mother’s attitude towards the father.

[
69
]

Being older, they are more able to recognize and
appreciate their father’s contribution, his qualities and his role as a father.
They also seem more able to express discomfort or assert opposition to a parent
when badmouthing of the other parent occurs.

[
70
]

However, according to the evidence, this
apparent balance is still very fragile. The episode concerning the affidavits
signed last fall is very revealing and should never have occurred.

[
71
]

It is clear from the proof that the mother’s
attitude is the least changed of all. She still does not seem to grasp that she
is not the victim and that the situation she so strongly denounces as causing
distress to the children is mainly brought about by herself, by her refusal to
encourage the importance of a meaningful relationship with both parents.

[
72
]

The Court remains sensitive to X and Y’s needs
and wishes which they expressed with candour and courage. Their position is legitimate,
seeing their fondness for their mother and their need for her increased presence
at this time in their lives.

[
73
]

However, as the Court told the parties when the
hearing was completed on April 19, the evidence does not allow it to conclude
that at this time, it is in the best interest of the children to award their
full custody to the mother, nor even to entertain joint custody.

[
74
]

After having reflected upon the evidence,
including the expert reports, the Court will maintain custody to the father but
will modify and extend the duration, although slightly, of the mother’s access periods.

[
75
]

At this time, the evidence shows that the risk
of estrangement of the father is still very present. The progress made by the
children with regard to recognizing his contribution has struck a delicate balance.
The fact that they are now more able to discern their needs as concerns both
parents, as opposed to their mother’s wishes in this respect, should not be jeopardized.

[
76
]

The Court will therefore grant the mother three consecutive
weekends out of five, from the Friday at 5 pm unto the Sunday at 5 pm,
including any pedagogical or statutory holiday immediately preceding or
following the weekend.

[
77
]

The mother will have phone access every
Wednesday between 7 and 7:45 pm, the father having to ensure that the children
are made available for this.

[
78
]

On the Wednesday evenings during the two week period
when the mother has no access rights during the weekends, instead of a phone call,
she will be allowed to pick up the children at school and return them home to
their father by 8 pm.

[
79
]

The mother will have two consecutive weeks
during the summer period. She will have priority of choice of weeks on even
years and must advise the father of her choice at the latest by June 1
st

of said year, and vice versa for the father.

[
80
]

The Jewish Holidays will be divided equally between
the parents.

[
81
]

The father will be allowed to travel with the
children to Mexico for two consecutive weeks during the Holidays, without prior
authorization from the mother. Should this intervene in the mother’s sequence
of access rights, the mother will be allowed an additional weekend prior to or
after the Holidays, at her choice.

[
82
]

Spring break will be shared on an alternating
basis, the mother having the even years and the father the odd years.

[
83
]

When the children are with the mother, including
during holiday periods, the father will have unrestricted communication access
to them but may phone them no more than once a day. The mother will be ordered
to ensure that the children are made available for this and will be ordered not
to intervene in the communications between the father and the children. The
children will be allowed to contact their father as often as they want and the
mother will be ordered not to prevent this.

[
84
]

When asked how to restrict e-mails, text
messages and Facebook contacts by the children with their mother when the
children are with the father, neither Mr Blais, nor anyone else, was able to enlighten
the Court on how to achieve this.

[
85
]

Therefore, seeing the importance of this issue
in the present circumstances, the Court will order the mother to discourage the
children from communicating with her in this manner and to rather channel and
limit them to the weekly Wednesday phone call.

[
86
]

The parents should exercise joint parental
authority. The Court will order that they advise each other should any urgent
issue arise concerning the children’s health or welfare.

[
87
]

Notwithstanding the sequence of custody or
access rights, the children will be with their father on Father’s day and with
their mother on Mother’s day.

[
88
]

Both parents will be ordered to communicate
travel arrangements, copies of airline tickets and itineraries, together with
coordinates of where they will be residing or may be reached while out of the
country with the children, at least three weeks prior to the date of departure.

[
89
]

Except for the father’s travel to Mexico with the children, the written authorization of the other parent will be required
for travelling out of the country. In case of disagreement, the Court will have
to decide.

[
90
]

The Court will order that both parents sign the
applicable requests concerning passport issuance or renewal for the children
but that the father will be responsible for processing said requests. Should
the mother refuse, the father will be allowed to proceed without her signature.

[
91
]

As this was not addressed in the father’s
proceedings and as the proof on this issue was inconclusive, the father’s
request concerning the remittal by the mother of savings bonds to the benefit
of the children is referred to the February hearing. The Court encourages the
parties to settle this amicably in the meantime, in the best interest of the
children.

[
92
]

The Court also strongly suggests that therapy
for the children be maintained and  that both parents seek help in attaining
co-parenting skills.

[
93
]

Most of all, the Court strongly recommends that
the mother seek and resume professional help in attaining insight on the
importance for the children to develop and maintain a significant and steadfast
relationship with both parents, notwithstanding the separation.

[
94
]

Finally, seeing that the entirety of the
mother’s amended motion in modification of accessory measures was not debated,
leaving the issue of provision for costs, together with the father’s amended
motion to have mother’s pleadings declared improper and to impose sanctions for
abusive proceedings to also be decided, the Court does not intend to dispose of
costs at this time. This will be referred to the February 2014 hearing, as the
Court is of the opinion that these outstanding issues are intimately related.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
95
]

MAINTAINS
the
custody of X and Y with the father;

[
96
]

As of the date of this judgment
, GRANTS
the
following access rights to the mother and
ORDERS
the father to respect
them:

-           starting
May 17, 2013, three consecutive weekends out of five, from the Friday at 5 pm
unto the Sunday at 5 pm, including any pedagogical or statutory holiday immediately
preceding or following the weekend;

-           phone
access every Wednesday between 7 and 7:45 pm and
ORDERS
the father to
ensure that the children are made available for this;

-

on the Wednesday evenings during the two-week
period when the mother has no access rights during the weekends, instead of a
phone call,
ALLOWS
the mother to pick up the children at school and
ORDERS

the mother to return them home to their father by 8 pm;

-

two consecutive weeks during the summer period,
the mother having priority of choice of weeks on even years;
ORDERS
the
mother to advise the father of her choice at the latest by June 1
st
of
said year and
ORDERS
that these modalities also apply to the father in
the odd years;

-

half of the Jewish Holidays;

-

spring break in the even years;

-

and according to any other time or modality as agreed
upon amicably by the parties;

[
97
]

AUTHORIZES
the
father to travel with the children to Mexico for two consecutive weeks during
the Holidays, without prior authorization from the mother; should this intervene
in the mother’s sequence of access rights,
GRANTS
an additional weekend of
access to the mother, prior to or after the Holidays, at her choice;

[
98
]

ORDERS
that when
the children are with the mother, including during holiday periods, the father
will have unrestricted communication access to them but may phone them no more
than once a day;
ORDERS
the mother to ensure that the children are made
available for this and
ORDERS
the mother not to intervene in the
communications between the father and the children;

[
99
]

ORDERS
that the
children be allowed to contact their father at all times and as often as they
want and
ORDERS
the mother not to prevent this;

[
100
]

ORDERS
the mother
to discourage the children from communicating with her by e-mail, text messages
or Facebook contacts and to rather channel and limit them to the weekly
Wednesday phone call access;

[
101
]

ORDERS
both
parents not to denigrate or provoke each other in front of the children, nor to
criticize the conduct and behaviour of the other parent in front of the children,
nor to tolerate that third parties do so in front of them;

[
102
]

ORDERS
both
parents to keep the children out of their personal and financial disputes and
to avoid discussing such with them;

[
103
]

DECLARES
that the
parents exercise joint parental authority;

[
104
]

ORDERS
that both
parents advise each other should any urgent issue arise concerning the children’s
health or welfare;

[
105
]

Notwithstanding the sequence of custodial or
access rights,
ORDERS
that the children will be with their father on
Father’s day and with their mother on Mother’s day;

[
106
]

ORDERS
both parents to communicate
travel arrangements, copies of airline tickets and itineraries, together with
coordinates of where they will be residing or may be reached while out of the
country with the children, at least three weeks prior to the date of departure;

[
107
]

Except for the father’s travel to Mexico with
the children which he can do without prior authorization from the mother,
ORDERS

that the written authorization of the other parent be obtained for travelling
elsewhere out of the country;

[
108
]

ORDERS
that both
parents sign the applicable requests concerning passport issuance or renewal
for the children and
ORDERS
that the father be responsible for
processing said requests;

[
109
]

ORDERS
that should
the mother refuse in cases of the above paragraphs [107] and [108], the father
will be allowed to proceed without her signature;

[
110
]

RESERVES
the
father’s rights as pertains to child support for the benefit of X and Y;

[
111
]

REFERS
the father’s
request concerning the remittal by the mother of savings bonds to the benefit
of the children to the February 20 and 21, 2014 hearing and
ENCOURAGES
the
parties to settle this issue amicably in the meantime, in the best interest of
the children;

[
112
]

strongly
recommends
that the mother seek and resume
professional help in attaining insight on the importance for the children to
develop and maintain a significant and steadfast relationship with both
parents, notwithstanding the separation;

[
113
]

strongly recommends
that therapy for the children be maintained;

[
114
]

STRONGLY

urges
both parents to seek help and
enrol in lectures or seminars on co-parenting to improve their cooperation and
communication skills as concerns their children;

[
115
]

COSTS to follow
.

__________________________________
